dossier.public_summary: TESS sees five brief dips in one sector with odd and even depths differing by 3.4 sigma and one dip much shallower than the others. The signal comes from the target star and looks flat and planet-sized, but the depth changes from transit to transit are far too large for a planet. Together with the odd-even mismatch this matches a binary or spot-crossing false alarm on the target, not a stable planetary transit.

reasons.why: Five transits are not consistent; two deep ~3900 ppm and one ~65 ppm outlier drive the signal with 99% in the top three. One transit is essentially missing (65 ppm) - inconsistent with a planet on target.
reasons.value: mean_depth_ppm=1892, chi2=75.89431760441164 dof=4 p_consistent=1.2889441793359034e-15, share_of_top_3=0.991, outliers=3913 ppm sigma=4.9, 65 ppm sigma=-4.4, 3708 ppm sigma=4.4

reasons.why: Odd and even eclipses differ by 4x at 3.44 sigma (sector_oe_max_sigma=3.441, sector_oe_sectors_over_3=1, sector_oe_same_sign_share=1). Over five events this is reported as odd/even difference favoring a binary at twice the period.
Centroid puts the dip on the target (suspects >4.3 sigma away) and rules out neighbours, so an EB on the target is still favored over a blend.
Flat-bottomed and duration fit a K dwarf, and size is planet-like, which alone does not prove a planet - a grazing small-star EB can also be flat and similarly sized.
Low planet_rank and similar candidates with not a planet/blend/false alarm outcomes support the EB/false-alarm interpretation over a planet.
